newsitem.title: Italy: Italy, France and Germany deny EMU "secret deal".
newsitem.headline: Italy, France and Germany deny EMU "secret deal".

text.p: Italy, Germany and France denied on Wednesday there were any "secret deals" to keep Italy out of the start of Europe's planned single currency.

Italian Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi rejected an Italian newspaper report that France and Germany were negotiating to bar Italy and Spain from the first wave of countries hoping to join economic and monetary union (EMU).
"I exclude that there are prejudicial attitudes against Italy and that there are secret accords," Ciampi said in response to the report that a deal was in the works.
In Bonn, German Finance Minister Theo Waigel denied any such plan existed. "All countries that qualify will be able to participate in the first round.
"Otherwise they will be able to participate when they qualify and no member will be arbitrarily excluded," he said.
A French finance ministry official called the report in the business daily Il Sole 24 Ore "totally absurd".

Il Sole, quoting "sources in Bonn", said France had come round to the idea of keeping Italy and Spain out of the group of EMU founders. This was because it feared Germany would otherwise insist on a two-year delay in the currency's planned January 1999 launch.
"Since it is considered politically too risky to abandon Italy as the only excluded one together with Greece, (the idea of) similar treatment for Spain is gaining ground," it added.

Italy is struggling to wrestle its public sector borrowing requirement down to three percent of gross domestic product by the end of the year in an effort to meet tough economic criteria for joining EMU.

But doubts remain as to whether Italy's recent deficit-cutting measures will have a lasting effect on state accounts, with two international organisations voicing their concerns in reports on Tuesday.
The Paris-based Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development said Italy must make structural reforms to state spending to keep the lid on its budget deficit in future.
In Frankfurt, the European Monetary Institute (EMI), the forerunner of a European central bank, criticised countries which took one-off measures to cut deficits.

It mentioned no country by name but economists took it to mean Italy, which has resorted to a special "Euro-tax" and revenue-raising measures in its 1997 budget and a recent supplementary budget for this year to keep the deficit in check.
Ciampi acknowledged the doubts on Wednesday, saying Italy's effort to slash its deficit-GDP ratio by around four percentage points from 1996 to 1997 was "some undertaking".
"Certainly there are doubts about Italy's capacity to reach the criteria and above all the doubt that Italy will be capable of remaining inside (EMU)," he told reporters.

But it was important to have as many countries joining the euro as possible. "The strength of the (euro) is not so much a matter of how small it will be or how close to the deutschemark but how broad it will be," Ciampi said.

The centre-left government wants to tackle the structural problem of welfare spending, in particular its bloated pensions bill. But it faces stiff resistance from its key ally in parliament, the hard-left Communist Refoundation party.
Ciampi stressed that corrections to state spending would have to be made in the end. "There are deadlines which force us into these corrective measures. The sooner they happen the better," he said.
In addition the timetable for the start of EMU was set. "We must do our utmost to win the confidence of our people and our European friends," Ciampi said.
